Lesson Overview: Author Presentation of Creative Work

Lesson Focus

Lesson 6: Author Presentation of Creative Work

Primary Standard: MLA.CW.COM.01 — Author presentation of creative work.

Supporting Standards: MLA.CW.WR.08 — Reflection on creative process and product; MLA.CW.COM.03 — Communication of craft reasoning.

What You Will Learn

  • Frame a creative work for an audience without explaining away its meaning.
  • Select two or three craft choices worth discussing.
  • Connect revision evidence to purpose and reader effect.
  • Deliver a concise, confident author introduction and reflection.

Why This Matters

Creative writing helps you communicate ideas, experiences, and perspectives with purpose. Each lesson strengthens your ability to read like a writer, make deliberate craft choices, revise thoughtfully, and explain how those choices affect a reader. These skills build creative confidence, clear communication, and responsible participation in a writing community.

What You Will Do

  • Learn and apply the lesson vocabulary.
  • Follow step-by-step instruction and study worked examples.
  • Practice through interactive checks and guided application.
  • Complete Independent Work to apply the lesson skills.
  • Complete a separate Checkpoint to demonstrate your understanding.

Lesson Workflow

  1. Complete Pages 1–4 in order.
  2. Complete Page 5 and submit it with your Page 2 vocabulary in Notebook Evidence Submission.
  3. Complete Page 6 and submit it separately in Checkpoint Submission.
  4. Review TOR feedback, correct errors, and resubmit any work scoring below 80%.
  5. Complete the assessment listed after the lesson. A score of at least 80% is required.

page.title: Vocabulary and Definitions
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 6 | Page 2 of 6

Vocabulary and Definitions

Notebook Task: Record every core term and its complete meaning in your notebook. Submit these vocabulary notes with your Independent Work as Notebook Evidence. Use the examples to see how each term works in context. Reference glossary terms do not need to be copied.
TermMeaningExample
author statementA brief explanation that frames a creative work and identifies purposeful craft decisions.The author statement explains why the story uses an unreliable narrator.
framingThe context an author gives an audience before presenting a work.The speaker introduces the setting before reading the excerpt.
craft choiceA deliberate decision about language, structure, imagery, voice, pacing, or form.Repeating the river image is a craft choice that unifies the poem.
audience effectThe response, question, feeling, or understanding a writer intends to create.The abrupt ending is meant to leave the audience unsettled.
rationaleA clear explanation of why a decision was made.The writer gives a rationale for selecting the opening scene.
excerptA short selected passage from a longer work.The presenter reads a two-paragraph excerpt from the memoir.
deliveryThe use of pace, volume, emphasis, posture, and eye contact while presenting.A slower pace and pause emphasize the final line.
reflectionCareful thinking about a process, its results, and possible next steps.The reflection names what improved and what the writer will revise next.

Vocabulary in Action

Match each clue to the precise term. Choose Check, study any mismatch, and retry. This practice is ungraded.

Make the Vocabulary Work

Which author-statement sentence gives a clear rationale?

A. “I chose this excerpt because it is my favorite.”

This gives a preference but does not connect the choice to craft or audience effect.

B. “I chose the opening excerpt because its repeated river image introduces the conflict and prepares listeners for the ending.”

Correct. It explains the craft-based reason and the intended audience effect.

page.title: Lesson
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 6 | Page 3 of 6

Lesson: Build an Author Presentation

The Core Principle

An author presentation is not a plot summary and not a defense of every sentence. It is a curated window into intention and revision. Curated means carefully selected for a purpose.

The FRAME Process

  1. F — Focus: Name the work, genre, and central creative aim in one sentence.
  2. R — Read: Choose a brief excerpt that reveals a significant craft decision.
  3. A — Analyze: Point to exact words, structure, image, or rhythm in the excerpt.
  4. M — Make the connection: Explain how the choice supports purpose and audience effect.
  5. E — Evaluate revision: Compare an earlier decision with the final one and name what improved.

Pause and Choose: Move from Intent to Evidence

Which presentation statement best explains a craft decision?

A. “I wanted the scene to feel tense, and I think it turned out really well.”
Weaker choice. The speaker names an intention and gives self-praise but offers no textual evidence or explanation of the reader’s experience.
B. “I shortened the final three sentences and repeated ‘closer’ so the pace accelerates as the threat approaches.”
Stronger choice. It identifies exact structural and language choices, connects them to pacing, and explains the intended audience effect.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Presentation Map

Context
20–30 sec
→
Excerpt
30–60 sec
→
Craft reasoning
60–90 sec
→
Revision reflection
30–45 sec

Delivery Rehearsal

Listen forRevise by
RushingMark two purposeful pauses.
Vague claimsUnderline the exact evidence you will name.
OverexplainingCut summary that does not support a craft claim.

Pause and Choose: Curate the Excerpt

The writer has four minutes to present a ten-page story. Which excerpt should the writer choose?

A. A short passage that clearly demonstrates the craft decision the writer will analyze and compare with an earlier version.
Stronger choice. A curated excerpt is selected for explanatory value. It gives listeners enough evidence to follow the reasoning without replacing the presentation with a long reading.
B. The first four minutes of the story, even if the relevant revision appears later.
Weaker choice. Chronological order is not the goal. An excerpt that does not support the craft claim uses time without deepening the audience’s understanding.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Common Mistakes

  • Summary trap: retelling events instead of explaining a decision.
  • Intent without evidence: saying “I wanted it to feel tense” without showing how language creates tension.
  • Empty praise: calling a choice “effective” without naming an audience effect.
  • Revision list: naming changes without explaining why the final choice is stronger.

page.title: Worked Example
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 6 | Page 4 of 6

Worked Example: Three Author Presentations

Example 1 — Image and Restraint

Draft excerpt: “The hospital corridor was very quiet and scary, and Mara felt afraid.”

Revision: “The corridor swallowed the squeak of Mara’s shoes.”

  1. Focus: The scene presents fear through restrained description.
  2. Evidence: The verb swallowed personifies the corridor; the single sound makes the silence concrete.
  3. Effect: Readers infer Mara’s fear rather than being told.
  4. Revision rationale: The revision replaces labels with sensory evidence and trusts the reader.

Model presentation line: “I removed the emotional labels so one image could carry both silence and threat.”

Pause and Choose: A or B

Which presentation statement most clearly explains the revision’s craft and effect?

A. I made the sentence better by adding stronger imagery.
Weaker response. This evaluates the revision without identifying what changed or how the reader’s experience changed.
B. I removed the emotional labels and personified the corridor as swallowing one small sound, allowing readers to infer both silence and threat.
Stronger response. This response names the deletion, the new device and evidence, and the intended inferential effect.

Retry: Close your first choice and open the other. Compare both explanations before continuing.

Example 2 — Pacing Through Syntax

Excerpt: “He found the key. Turned it. Waited. Nothing.”

  1. Focus: A character expects a consequence that does not arrive.
  2. Evidence: Fragments and one-word sentences compress time, then the final word creates a stop.
  3. Effect: The audience experiences each action and the uneasy pause.
  4. Delivery choice: Read the first three units steadily, pause, then lower volume on “Nothing.”

Model presentation line: “I broke grammatical completeness on purpose because the character’s attention has narrowed to separate beats.”

Example 3 — Symbol and Revision

Early version: A cracked teacup appears once on a kitchen counter.

Final version: The cup appears at the opening, is repaired with visible gold resin midway, and is offered to an estranged sister at the close.

  1. Focus: The story explores repair that does not erase damage.
  2. Evidence: Repetition turns the cup into a motif; the visible seam parallels the sisters’ relationship.
  3. Effect: The final gesture suggests cautious reconciliation without claiming everything is fixed.
  4. Revision rationale: Repetition and placement transform a prop into structural meaning.

Model presentation line: “I revised the cup from decoration into a recurring motif, so its changed condition tracks the relationship.”

Transfer Pattern

For your own work, complete this chain: Exact choice → textual evidence → intended effect → revision reason. If any link is missing, the explanation is incomplete.

Your Turn Before Independent Work

Pause and try: Prepare one presentation sentence for revising “The room was lonely” to “One cup cooled beside the untouched plate.”

Check your thinking — open after you try
Teacher model: I replaced the emotional label with two unattended objects; the cooling cup and untouched plate make absence visible and allow readers to infer loneliness.

page.title: Independent Work
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 6 | Page 5 of 6

Independent Work: Author Presentation of Creative Work

Purpose

Present creative work with purposeful selection, clear context, expressive delivery planning, and respect for the audience.

Complete each numbered part in your notebook. Use precise evidence from your own work and the source provided.

Source for Your Work

Presentation situation: You have three minutes to introduce and read part of a piece to an audience unfamiliar with your work. Your goal is to create context without explaining away the piece.

1. Plan Before You Work

DecisionYour Plan
Purpose and intended audienceState each clearly.
Most important craft or communication needName the need and evidence.
Success indicatorDescribe what an effective result will do for a reader.

2. Choose and Explain

Which approach demonstrates stronger decision-making? Record A or B, then explain your choice in 2–3 sentences using a lesson concept.

A. Summarize every event and explain the theme before reading so the audience cannot misunderstand.
B. Offer only the context the audience needs, select a revealing excerpt, and plan delivery choices that support the writing.

3. Apply the Lesson

Create a three-minute author-presentation script containing a concise introduction, a 250–350 word excerpt or 20–28 lines, and a closing reflection. Add delivery annotations for pace, pause, emphasis, and eye contact.

4. Revise with Purpose

Read the script aloud. Revise one transition and two delivery annotations, then explain how the changes improve audience understanding or engagement.

Before You Submit

  • All four numbered parts are complete.
  • Your work applies the lesson skill to a specific creative product.
  • Your explanation identifies a decision and its effect on readers.
  • Your revision meaningfully improves the work, not only its appearance.
TOR Help
Contact your Teacher of Record if you need clarification, feedback, or support before submitting your work.

page.title: Checkpoint
page.contents:
Checkpoint: Author Presentation of Creative Work

Put the lesson together through analysis, decision-making, writing, and purposeful revision.

Purpose

Show that you can understand the lesson concept, apply it in original work, and explain your decisions. Complete every numbered item and submit your responses with your Checkpoint work.

New Source: Two Openings

Opening A: “Here is my story. I wrote it for class. I hope you like it.”

Opening B: “When I drafted ‘The Last Bus,’ I wanted readers to feel how one ordinary delay can expose a difficult choice. Listen for the repeated image of the clock; it changes meaning after the turning point.”

An author presentation introduces a work, establishes context and purpose, delivers an effective excerpt, and reflects on craft for a specific audience.

Part 1: Analyze the Source

  1. Why does Opening B better prepare the audience to understand the work? Identify two purposeful elements.
  2. What should an author explain before an excerpt, and what should remain for the excerpt itself to reveal?

Use this response pattern: Make a precise claim, cite the relevant detail, and explain how the detail proves the claim.

Part 2: Choose A or B

3. Which presentation plan respects both audience needs and the creative work?

A. Summarize every event and explain the theme before reading so the audience cannot misunderstand.
B. Provide concise context and a listening purpose, then let a well-chosen excerpt demonstrate the craft and meaning.

Record A or B in your submission and explain your choice in 2–3 sentences. The answer is not revealed here because this item is part of your graded written work.

Part 3: Create and Apply

4. Create a 4–6 minute author presentation for one original work.

  1. Opening: Hook the audience; name the title, form, purpose, and intended audience.
  2. Context: Give only the information needed to understand the selected excerpt.
  3. Reading: Choose and mark a 2–3 minute excerpt; annotate pauses, emphasis, and pacing.
  4. Craft reflection: Explain two intentional choices and one substantive revision.
  5. Closing: Synthesize what you want the audience to carry away and invite one focused question.

Submit the complete speaking script and the marked excerpt.

Plan before drafting: Decide what the audience should understand, how each section will build that understanding, and which details will do the most work.

Part 4: Revise With Purpose

5. Practice aloud with a timer. Revise one section for clarity and one delivery note for emphasis or pacing; explain both changes.

Do more than correct spelling. Revise organization, meaning, evidence, or craft so the work becomes clearer and more effective.

Before You Submit

  • Every numbered item is complete.
  • Analysis includes specific evidence and reasoning.
  • The creative work follows the required organization and length.
  • The A/B response is recorded and explained.
  • The revision is visible and its purpose is clear.

Mastery Target

A score of 80% or higher demonstrates mastery. Depth, control, and application matter more than unnecessary length.

TOR Help

If you are unsure how to organize your response, choose evidence, or revise meaningfully, contact your Teacher of Record before submitting.
